name: Action / Platformer
description: Tight movement and combat through hand-built levels, each with the code that makes it feel right and the assets it needs.

pillars.name: Responsive Control
pillars.feeling: the character does exactly what I meant, instantly

pillars.name: Mastery Through Practice
pillars.feeling: I get visibly better every attempt

pillars.name: Every Screen a Challenge
pillars.feeling: each room is a new test of what I've learned

gameExamples.heading: Pitch
gameExamples.text: A tight 2.5D platformer where a nimble hero dashes and wall-jumps through hand-built gauntlets.

gameExamples.heading: Core Loop
gameExamples.text:
1. Enter a room.
2. Read its hazards and enemies.
3. Clear it with movement and attacks.
4. Reach the checkpoint and the next room.

gameExamples.heading: Non-goals
gameExamples.text:
- Procedurally generated levels.
- Inventory management.
- Long cutscenes.

docs.title: Movement
docs.summary: How the player runs, jumps and traverses; the verb everything else is built around.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can run, jump and change direction mid-air.
- As a player, I can chain moves together without stopping.
- As a player, I can recover from a mistake mid-jump.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- The character squashes and stretches on landing.
- Dust and sound on every jump and landing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Input is buffered for a few frames.
- Jumping a few frames after leaving a ledge still works (coyote time).

docs.title: Run and Jump
docs.summary: Ground speed, acceleration, jump arcs, coyote time and input buffering.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can control jump height by holding the button.
- As a player, I can reach full speed quickly.
- As a player, I can land precisely on small platforms.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A clear landing shadow under the character.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Releasing jump early cuts the jump short.
- Air control is slightly lower than ground control.

docs.title: Dash
docs.summary: Burst movement: distance, cooldown and how it chains with other moves.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can dash in any direction.
- As a player, I can dash through some hazards.
- As a player, I can chain a dash into a jump.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A trail behind the character during the dash.
- The dash icon dims while it recharges.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- One dash in the air; it recharges on landing.
- The dash makes the player invulnerable for its first frames.

docs.title: Wall Interactions
docs.summary: Wall slides, wall jumps, ledge grabs and climbing.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can slide down walls.
- As a player, I can jump off walls.
- As a player, I can grab ledges and climb up.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Particles where the character touches the wall.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Wall slides slow the fall.
- Wall jumps push away from the wall.

docs.title: Character Movement
docs.summary: The movement component: physics, input buffering, coyote time and tuning values.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A custom movement component on top of the character movement component adds coyote time, jump buffering, variable jump height, dash and wall interactions. All tuning values come from a data asset so designers can tweak them live.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UPlatformerMovementComponent`: adds the custom movement modes
- `UMovementTuning`: data asset with every tuning value

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Speeds, gravity, jump heights and timings in UMovementTuning.
- Coyote time and buffer windows in frames.

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: A bright, readable hero who stands out against every background.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Stylized characters with strong silhouettes.
- Animation packs with platformer moves (double jump, wall slide, dash).

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Realistic proportions.
- Dark color schemes that blend into backgrounds.

docs.title: Combat
docs.summary: How the player fights: attacks, hits and damage.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can attack, dodge and block with simple inputs.
- As a player, I can read what an enemy is about to do.
- As a player, I can feel each hit land.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Wind-up animations before enemy attacks.
- Hit flashes, sounds and a short pause on impact.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every enemy attack can be avoided.
- Damage numbers stay small enough to reason about.

docs.title: Attacks
docs.summary: The player's attacks, combos and their timing windows.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can attack in a short combo.
- As a player, I can attack in the air.
- As a player, I can cancel an attack into a dash.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Weapon trails on each swing.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Combos have three hits.
- Attacks can be cancelled into a dash but not into a jump.

docs.title: Hit Reactions
docs.summary: Knockback, hitstun, invulnerability frames and feedback on both sides of a hit.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can see when I've been hit and how badly.
- As a player, I can get a moment to recover after being hit.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- The character flashes and is knocked back.
- A short freeze on heavy hits.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- After a hit the player is invulnerable for one second.
- Knockback never pushes the player into a pit.

docs.title: Combat System
docs.summary: Hitboxes, damage events, hitstop and invulnerability in code.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Attacks enable hitbox components on specific animation frames through anim notifies. Overlaps send damage through the damage interface; a short hitstop pauses both actors.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UHitboxComponent`: enabled by anim notifies, detects overlaps
- `UCombatComponent`: combos, cancels and hitstop

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Attack timings in animation notifies.
- Damage values and hitstop lengths in data assets.

docs.title: Combat Effects
docs.summary: Hit VFX, impact sounds and camera shakes.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Hit sparks | VFX | Placeholder | To source |
| Impact sounds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Camera shakes | Data | Placeholder | To source |
| Death effects | VFX | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Short, bright and readable: effects confirm a hit without hiding the next threat.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Niagara VFX packs with hits, slashes and explosions.
- Impact sound libraries with light, medium and heavy variations.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Long-lasting particles that clutter the screen.
- Effects in a different style from the characters.

docs.title: Camera
docs.summary: How the camera follows, frames and leads the action.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: A spring-arm camera follows the player with a small dead zone and leads in the direction of movement. Camera volumes in levels override framing for special rooms.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `APlatformerCameraManager`: follow, lead and dead zone
- `ACameraVolume`: per-room framing overrides

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Follow speeds and lead distance in a data asset.
- Volume settings on each camera volume.

docs.title: Levels
docs.summary: Hand-built levels that teach, test and reward the player's moves.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can move through each level and always know where to go next.
- As a player, I can find side paths that reward curiosity.
- As a player, I can see where I've been and where I haven't.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- Landmarks visible from far away.
- Light and color that guide me toward the main path.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every level has a clear start, goal and one optional reward.
- Levels teach a new idea before testing it.

docs.title: Checkpoints
docs.summary: Where the player respawns and how much progress a death costs.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can respawn close to where I died.
- As a player, I can see when I've reached a checkpoint.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A checkpoint lights up when reached.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every room has a checkpoint at its entrance.
- Collectibles picked up since the checkpoint are kept.

docs.title: Hazards
docs.summary: Spikes, pits, moving platforms and other environmental dangers.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can recognize a hazard before touching it.
- As a player, I can use some hazards against enemies.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Hazards use one warning color across the game.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Touching a hazard costs one heart.
- Pits respawn the player at the last safe ground.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.summary: Hidden areas and collectibles that reward mastery and exploration.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can find hidden rooms.
- As a player, I can collect secrets to unlock extras.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A subtle visual hint near every secret.
- A counter of secrets found per level.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every level has three secrets.
- Secrets are never required to finish the game.

docs.title: Level Kit
docs.summary: Tiles, platforms, props and backgrounds the levels are built from.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:

| Decor props | Mesh | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Foreground, gameplay and background layers are clearly separated by value and saturation.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Modular platformer kits on a grid.
- Parallax background packs.
- Packs with matching hazards (spikes, saws).

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Busy backgrounds with the same contrast as platforms.
- Kits without collision-friendly shapes.

docs.title: Enemies
docs.summary: What the player fights, and how each one tests a different skill.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can learn each enemy's pattern.
- As a player, I can defeat enemies in more than one way.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - Each enemy telegraphs its attack with a pose and a sound.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Each enemy type tests one skill (jumping, timing, positioning).
- Enemies don't respawn until the checkpoint is reset.

docs.title: Bosses
docs.summary: Multi-phase encounters that test everything the player has learned.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can learn a boss over several attempts.
- As a player, I can see how close the boss is to defeat.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text: - A boss health bar with phase markers.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Bosses have three phases.
- Each phase adds one new attack.

docs.title: Enemy AI
docs.summary: Behavior trees or state machines, attack patterns and spawning.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Simple enemies use state machines (patrol, chase, attack); bosses use behavior trees with one subtree per phase.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `AEnemyBase`: health, state machine and attacks
- `BT_Boss`: the boss behavior tree

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Patrol paths placed in levels.
- Attack patterns in data assets.

docs.title: Enemy Assets
docs.summary: Enemy and boss meshes, animations and sounds.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:

|---|---|---|---|

| Enemy animations | Animation | Placeholder | To source |
| Enemy sounds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Each enemy type has a distinct silhouette and color so the player recognizes it instantly.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Creature packs with idle, move, attack, hit and death animations.
- Packs with several variants on one skeleton.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Enemies that look like the player or allies.
- Animation sets missing hit or death animations.

docs.title: UI
docs.summary: Menus and HUD: what the player sees and can do outside the game world.

examples.heading: The Player Can
examples.text:
- As a player, I can start, pause and quit from clear menus.
- As a player, I can change graphics, audio and control settings.
- As a player, I can see the information I need during play without it covering the action.

examples.heading: The Player Sees
examples.text:
- A title screen, pause menu and settings screens.
- A HUD with only what matters right now.
- Button prompts that match my input device.

examples.heading: Rules
examples.text:
- Every screen can be used with a gamepad as well as mouse and keyboard.
- Pausing stops gameplay time.
- Settings save immediately.

docs.title: UI Framework
docs.summary: How screens and widgets are built, opened, navigated and fed data.

examples.heading: How It Works
examples.text: Screens are UMG widgets pushed onto a stack by a UI manager subsystem. The top screen gets input; popping it returns to the one below. Gameplay talks to the HUD through events, never directly.

examples.heading: Code
examples.text:
- `UProjectUISubsystem`: owns the screen stack and opens and closes screens
- `UScreenWidget`: base class for every full screen (menus, settings)
- `UHUDWidget`: the in-game HUD; listens to gameplay events

examples.heading: Data
examples.text:
- Screen classes and their input modes in a data asset.
- Settings in the game user settings, saved per user.

docs.title: UI Art
docs.summary: Icons, fonts, panels and widget skins.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Fonts (headings, body) | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Panel and button skins | UI | Placeholder | To source |
| Input prompt icons | UI | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Clean and readable first: flat shapes, high contrast, one accent color. Icons share one line weight and perspective.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- UI kits with matching icons, buttons and panels.
- Fonts licensed for games, with the character sets we localize to.
- Input prompt packs covering keyboard, Xbox and PlayStation.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Mixing icon packs with different styles.
- Ornate frames that crowd the screen.
- Fonts that are hard to read at small sizes.

docs.title: Music and Sound
docs.summary: Music, sound effects and ambience, and where each is used.

examples.heading: Assets Needed
examples.text:
| Asset | Type | Status | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main theme | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| Gameplay loops | Music | Placeholder | To source |
| UI sounds (click, back, confirm) | Sound | Placeholder | To source |
| Ambience beds | Sound | Placeholder | To source |

examples.heading: Style
examples.text: Music sets the mood of each area; sound effects are short and punchy so they read over the music.

examples.heading: What to Look For
examples.text:
- Music packs with loopable stems.
- Sound effect libraries with variations of each sound.
- Licenses that allow commercial use and streaming.

examples.heading: What to Avoid
examples.text:
- Tracks that don't loop cleanly.
- Effects with long tails that muddy fast moments.
- Mixing many libraries with different loudness.
